Neha / Hannah / Asha —

High-level technical breakdown:

1) Where copies can exist after the incident
- Active region: logs and KV cache live in the customer's pinned region (US-west-2 for Nimble per account metadata).
- Short-lived service replicas: during incident response we sometimes snapshot traces to the on-prem controller region for debugging; those snapshots are transient (TTL-managed).
- Backups & snapshots: Automatic daily snapshots of model-serving state are kept in the account's region by default, but older snapshots may be replicated to the Redwood archival bucket in us-west-1 for cold storage (policy: cross-region replication for disaster recovery).
- Third-party integrations: if customer configured external log forwarding (e.g., S3 export or Splunk/Datadog), copies may exist outside Redwood and are not controlled by our deletion API.

2) Deletion timeline & proof-of-deletion process (customer-initiated, post-incident)
- Primary step: mark objects for deletion and create a legal hold token if requested.
- Active store purge: we schedule an expedited purge job that deletes objects and invalidates KV cache entries within 48 hours for active region objects (subject to in-flight requests).
- Replica & archive purge: archival buckets and cross-region replicas are queued for deletion and garbage-collected within 7–14 days depending on lifecycle cycles (Glacier-style transitions may extend this; we'll surface exact S3 lifecycle state).
- Immutable snapshots & backups: if an immutable snapshot (WORM) exists due to regulatory holds, we can remove access and render data unreadable (revoke KMS key) and provide attestation, but physical deletion may be bound by retention windows.
- Proof artifact: we provide a signed deletion report showing object identifiers, deletion timestamps, and KMS key rotations or revocations. Hashes of deleted object IDs can be provided for audit.

3) Forensics-only artifacts
- We do not routinely retain kernel core dumps or raw GPU device traces unless explicitly elevated to a forensics hold. If elevated, those artifacts are stored in an isolated bucket with restricted access and a documented chain-of-custody.
- Access window: artifacts under forensics hold remain accessible only to the investigation team and are scheduled for purge after the hold is released. Typical hold durations are 30–90 days unless legal requests extend them.

I'll attach the internal deletion playbook excerpt with the exact runbooks and the log purge job IDs used for audit.

—Karthik
Head of Runtime Engineering | Redwood Inference

Thanks — a few legal/controls clarifications to add for Nimble Health's auditors:

- Legal Hold vs Deletion Request: If Nimble places a legal hold related to an ongoing investigation, we will not perform irreversible deletions until the hold is released. Instead we will isolate the artifacts and prevent any lifecycle-based deletion. We record the hold as an immutable ticket with start/end timestamps.
- Attestation content: Attestations will include: list of object keys, deletion timestamp, operator IDs who executed the purge, and the signature of our compliance lead. We can also include the S3 lifecycle event ids where applicable.
- Cross-region notifications: We'll provide proactive notifications to Nimble's security contact before we touch replicas in other regions to allow them to pause any external processes that might re-ingest data.
- Exceptions: any copy forwarded to an external vendor (SIEM, partner) is out-of-band and we will provide a contact list for those endpoints so Nimble can follow up.

I'll draft the exact language for your auditors and include it in the attestation template.

-Hannah
